en: Sukeśa Bhāradvāja, Śaibya Satyakāma, Sauryāyaṇī Gārgya, Kausalya Āśvalāyana, Bhārgava Vaidarbhi, and Kabandhī Kātyāyana—these men were devoted to Brahman, grounded in Brahman, seeking the Supreme Brahman. Thinking, "He indeed will tell us all that," they approached the venerable Pippalāda with sacrificial fuel in their hands. 1.1.
That seer said to them: "Dwell for another year with austerity, celibacy, and faith. Then ask questions as you desire; if we understand, we shall explain everything to you.
Then Kabandhī Kātyāyana approached and asked: "Venerable sir, from what indeed are these creatures born? (1.3)
The breath, indeed, is the sun; the moon is wealth. For all this that is both formed and formless is wealth; therefore, form itself is wealth. 1.5.
The omniform, golden-hued Jātavedas, the ultimate refuge, the singular light that blazes;
he who possesses a thousand rays and exists in a hundred ways.
This sun rises as the vital breath of all creatures. 1.8.

Prajāpati is indeed the year. His two courses are the southern and the northern. Those who meditate upon that as "the performed sacrifice and pious works" (iṣṭāpūrta) win only the world of the moon; they indeed return again. Therefore, these seers desiring offspring set out upon the southern course. This, indeed, is wealth which is the path of the ancestors. 1.9.

Then, having sought the Self through austerity, celibacy, faith, and knowledge, they conquer the sun. This indeed is the abode of the vital breaths; this is the immortal, the fearless; this is the ultimate goal. From this they do not return—this is the cessation. Regarding this, there is this verse: 1.10.
They call him the five-footed father, the twelvefold, rich in moisture, in the further half of heaven;
and these others call him the far-seeing one in the lower region.
"In the seven-wheeled [chariot], they say it is fixed upon the six spokes. (1.11)

The month is indeed Prajāpati. Its dark fortnight is his wealth (rayi), and its bright fortnight is his vital breath (prāṇa). Therefore, these seers perform sacrifices during the bright fortnight, while others do so during the other.

Prajāpati is indeed day and night. His day is his vital breath (prāṇa), and his night is his wealth (rayi). Those who unite in sexual pleasure during the day spill their vital breath; when they unite in sexual pleasure at night, that is truly the practice of celibacy (brahmacarya). 1.13.
Food indeed is Prajāpati; from that, verily, comes this seed. Therefore these creatures are born. (1.14) Those who indeed observe this vow of Prajāpati produce a pair.
This is the world of Brahman for those in whom austerity and celibacy exist, and in whom truth is firmly established. (1.15)
For those in whom there is no falsehood of tongue and no deceit, that stainless world of Brahmā belongs. || 1.16 ||
Thus ends the first question.
Therefore, Bhārgava Vaidarbhi asked him: "Venerable sir, how many gods indeed sustain living beings? Which among them illuminate this? And who, moreover, is the most excellent of them? (2.1)

The most excellent Prāṇa said to them: "Do not fall into delusion. It is I alone who, having divided myself fivefold, support and sustain this body. They, however, remained without faith. 2.3.153–154.

Out of pride, he seemed to rise upward. As he was rising, all the others indeed rose; and as he settled down, all of them indeed settled down. Just as when the king-bee rises up, all the bees rise up, and when he settles down, all of them settle down—so it was with speech, mind, sight, and hearing. Delighted, they praised Prāṇa. 2.4.
This is the fire that burns; this is the sun; this is Parjanya, the bounteous Maghavan; this is Vāyu.
This is the earth, wealth, the god, and whatever is existent and non-existent, and that which is immortal. 2.5.
As the spokes are fixed in the nave of a wheel, everything is established in the vital breath (prāṇa):
the Ṛg verses, the Yajus formulas, the Sāman chants, the sacrifice, the ruling power (kṣatra), and the spiritual power (brahman). 2.6.
As Prajāpati you move within the womb; from you alone are you born again.
To you, O Prāṇa, these creatures bring tribute, for upon you they are established through their vital breaths.
You are the foremost bearer of offerings for the gods, the first ancestral oblation for the ancestors, the truth practiced by the seers, and you belong to the Atharvans and Aṅgirases. 2.8.
By your splendor, O Prāṇa, you are Indra; you are Rudra, the protector.
You move in the intermediate space; you are the Sun, the lord of lights. || 2.9 ||
But when you rain down, O Prāṇa, these creatures of yours abide in a state of bliss, thinking, "Food will come according to our desire. || 2.10 ||
O Vratya, you are the sole seer of vital breath, the consumer of all, the true lord;
we are the givers of the first [offering], and you, O Mātariśvan, are our father.
That form of yours which is established in speech, that which is in the ear, and that which is in the eye, and that which is extended throughout the mind—make it auspicious; do not depart from us.
"Everything here, even that which is established in the third heaven, is under the control of the vital breath (prāṇa).
Like a mother protecting her sons, protect us; grant us prosperity and wisdom. || 2.13 ||
Thus ends the second question.

Then Kausalya Āśvalāyana questioned him: "Venerable sir, from where is this vital breath (prāṇa) born? How does it enter this body? Or, having divided itself, how does it take its stand? By what means does it depart? How does it sustain the external, and how the internal? (3.1)
This vital breath is born from the self;
just as this shadow exists in a person, so is this [breath] extended within it.
By means of what is fashioned by the mind, it enters into this body. 3.3.

Just as a sovereign king appoints his officials, saying, "Rule over these villages, rule over those villages," even so this vital breath (prāṇa) assigns the other vital breaths each to their respective places. 3.4.

The apāna breath is established in the anus and the generative organ; the prāṇa breath itself is established in the eyes, ears, mouth, and nose. But the samāna breath is in the middle, for it carries this offered food equally [throughout the body]. Therefore, these become the seven flames. 3.5.

For this Self is in the heart. Herein are these one hundred and one channels; from each of them there are a hundred [sub-branches], and for each of those there are seventy-two thousand secondary branch-channels. Within these moves the *vyāna* breath. (3.6) Now, by means of one [channel] the *udāna* breath moves upward; it leads to a world of merit through merit, to a world of evil through evil, and to the world of men through both. (3.7)

The sun, indeed, rises as the external breath, for it sustains this breath of the eye. That deity which is in the earth, that one, having taken hold of the downward breath (*apāna*) of the person, [remains there]. That which is the space between [the eyes] is the equalizing breath (*samāna*). Vāyu is the pervasive breath (*vyāna*). 3.8.

By whatever thought that [person] possesses, by that he enters into the vital breath; the vital breath, joined with heat and together with the self, leads him to the world as it has been conceived. 3.10.
He who, knowing this, knows the vital breath—his offspring does not perish, and he becomes immortal. Regarding this, there is this verse: 3.11.

Having understood the fivefold nature of the vital breath—its origin, its arrival, its location, and its pervasive power—as well as its internal state, one partakes of the immortal; having understood it, one partakes of the immortal. 3.12.
Thus ends the third question.

Then Gārgya Sauryāyaṇī questioned him: "Venerable sir, what are those things that sleep in this person? What are those that remain awake in him? Which among them is the god who sees dreams? To whom does this pleasure belong? And in whom, finally, do they all become established? (4.1)

He said to him: "Just as, Gārgya, when the sun is setting, all its rays become unified in this orb of light and then spread out again as it rises, even so, indeed, all this becomes unified in the supreme deity, the mind. Therefore, at that time, this person does not hear, does not see, does not smell, does not taste, does not touch, does not speak, does not take, does not feel pleasure, and does not emit; he does not move—he is called 'one who sleeps. (4.2)

It is the fires of the vital breaths that remain awake in this city. Indeed, the apāna is the gārhapatya fire; the vyāna is the anvāhāryapacana fire; and because it is led forth from the gārhapatya, the prāṇa is the āhavanīya fire through that leading forth. 4.3.

That which carries these two, inhalation and exhalation, evenly is the *samāna*. The mind, indeed, is the sacrificer; the result of the sacrifice is the *udāna*. It leads this sacrificer day after day to Brahman. 4.4.

In this state, this deity experiences his own greatness: he beholds again and again what has been seen; he hears again and again the very same thing that has been heard; and he repeatedly re-experiences what was experienced in various places and directions. He sees everything—both the seen and the unseen, the heard and the unheard, the experienced and the unexperienced, the existent and the non-existent. He, as the All, sees all. 4.5.
When he is overcome by that light, then this deity does not see dreams; then, in this body, there is this bliss. 4.6.
Just as, my dear, birds settle upon a tree for their lodging, even so, indeed, all that settles in the supreme Self. 4.7.

Earth and the subtle essence of earth; water and the subtle essence of water; fire and the subtle essence of fire; air and the subtle essence of air; ether and the subtle essence of ether; the eye and the visible; the ear and the audible; the nose and the olfactory; the tongue and the sapid; the skin and the tangible; speech and the speakable; the hands and the graspable; the organ of generation and the object of pleasure; the anus and the excretable; the feet and the walkable; the mind and the thinkable; the intellect and the intelligible; the ego-sense and the object of ego-identification; the heart and the object of thought; radiance and the object to be illumined; and the vital breath and the object to be sustained. (4.8)

For this person is the seer, the toucher, the hearer, the smeller, the taster, the thinker, the knower, and the agent; he is the self consisting of consciousness. He is firmly established in the supreme, imperishable Self. 4.9

He attains the supreme Imperishable itself. He who, my dear, knows that shadowless, bodiless, bloodless, radiant Imperishable—he indeed becomes all-knowing and becomes everything. On this there is this verse: 4.10.
O gentle one, he who knows that imperishable wherein the conscious self, along with all the gods,
the vital breaths, and all beings are established—
[he knows Brahman].
He, the omniscient one, entered into everything. 4.11.
Thus ends the fourth question.
Then Śaibya Satyakāma questioned him: "Venerable sir, if someone among men were to meditate upon the syllable *oṃ* until the end of his life, which world indeed does he win by that? (5.1)
To him he said: "Satyakāma, this syllable *oṃ* is indeed both the higher and the lower Brahman. Therefore, the wise man follows one or the other by means of this very support. 5.2.

If he meditates on it as consisting of a single measure, being made conscious by that very [meditation], he quickly reaches the earth. The *Ṛg* verses lead him to the world of men. There, endowed with austerity, celibacy, and faith, he experiences greatness. 5.3.

Now, if he attains the mind by means of two measures, he is led up to the intermediate space by the Yajus formulas to the world of Soma. Having experienced splendor in the world of Soma, he returns again. 5.4.

Furthermore, he who meditates upon the supreme Puruṣa by means of this very syllable "Om" consisting of three measures, having attained union with the light in the sun, is liberated from evil just as a snake is freed from its skin. Thus indeed, being liberated from evil, he is led up by the Sāmans to the world of Brahman. From this mass of living beings, he beholds the Puruṣa dwelling in the city, who is higher than the high. Regarding this, there are these two verses: 5.5.1 The small, old lotus flower that has appeared within the heart—within that is a small inner space; within that is what is to be contemplated. 5.5.2 Within the heart, there is a space like a smokeless fire; it is bright, pure, and stainless. It is there that one sees the Puruṣa, who is self-luminous and free from all taints. He is the one who knows all, the knower of all things, the one who is all-knowing, and the source of all knowledge. He is the Puruṣa who dwells in the city. These are the two verses. 5.5.2–3.
Three measures, subject to death, are employed,
mutually joined and not separated,
in the external, internal, and intermediate activities.
The wise one does not waver when [the elements] are correctly applied. || 5.6 ||
That which the seers know as this [earth] through the *ṛg* verses, the intermediate space through the *yajus* formulas, and that [heaven] through the *sāman* chants—
he follows after it by means of the *oṃ* syllable as his very abode.
The wise one knows that which is peaceful, undecaying, immortal, fearless, and supreme. || 5.7 ||
Thus ends the fifth question.
He reflected: "Upon whose departure shall I depart? Or upon whose being established shall I be established? (6.3)

He created vital breath (prāṇa). From vital breath, he created faith, space, air, light, water, earth, the senses, mind, food; from food, vigor, austerity, sacred formulas, action, worlds, and within the worlds, names. 6.4.

Just as these rivers, flowing toward the ocean, reach the ocean and vanish; their names and forms are destroyed, and they are simply called "the ocean"—even so, for this seer, these sixteen parts, which have the Puruṣa as their goal, reach the Puruṣa and vanish; their names and forms are destroyed, and he is simply called "the Puruṣa. He becomes partless and immortal. Regarding this, there is this verse: 6.5.17–20 (The verses are omitted here as per instructions).
"Know that Puruṣa who is to be known, in whom the parts are established like the spokes in the nave of a wheel, so that death may not afflict you. (6.6)

He said to them: "I know only this much, that this is the supreme Brahman; there is nothing beyond this. They honored him, saying: "You indeed are our father, for you have carried us across to the further shore of ignorance. Homage to the supreme sages! Homage to the supreme sages!
Thus ends the sixth question.
Thus ends the Praśnopaniṣad.
